summary: This FATF report examines how criminals launder proceeds of environmental crime -- illegal logging/land clearing, illegal mining, and waste trafficking -- estimated at USD 110-281 billion annually. It finds heavy reliance on front and shell companies to co-mingle illicit and legitimate proceeds early in supply chains, trade-based fraud (false invoicing, false descriptions of goods, over/under valuation) to move money across borders, cash-intensive sectors and MVTS/hawala to pay rural labour, and offshore corporate structures with nominee/opaque beneficial owners, often enabled by corruption of officials issuing concessions and licences. It also notes convergence with tax crime, smuggling, human trafficking and, in some cases, terrorist/insurgent financing, and sets out case studies, risk indicators and priority actions for AML authorities and the private sector.

citations.quote: This FATF report shows the significant role of trade-based fraud and misuse of shell and front companies to launder gains from illegal logging, illegal mining, and waste trafficking.
Some criminals specialise in one or more environmental crimes, and rely on specialized networks to move the products and facilitate the financial flows.
criminals used front companies to co-mingle gains from illegal mining, logging and waste trafficking into their legitimate business accounts
criminals manipulated the prices of the domestic vanilla trade to help integrate the illicit proceeds from rosewood trafficking
They relied on shell companies located overseas to move funds back and forth under the guise of invoices for processing their waste.

the funds were obscured through a web of domestic shell companies that had been established by Designated Non-Financial Business and Professions (DNFBPs)... the named individual on the registry would be a nominee with only a loose connection to the ultimate underlying owner
For environmental crimes specifically, this could include mislabelling of hazardous waste or protected wood to conceal their real value.
Shipping documents were falsified to state that the cargo consisted of goods and raw materials, as opposed to waste.

it is common for timber, processed lumber, or gold, to be exported at below market prices, change ownership and Bill of Lading en route, often in a customs free trade zone, and is imported at recipient countries at higher declared values
criminals use the mining sector to both generate criminal proceeds through illegal mining, and to launder proceeds from other crimes using the cash-intensive nature of the industry
In 2014, individuals would bulk buy vanilla to drive the prices up to conceal co-mingling and integration of criminal gains, presented as legitimate earnings from vanilla.
Large cash withdrawals from financial institutions operating in rural areas that may be in proximity to illegal mining or logging areas.

indicators.description: Use of front or shell companies (often related-party or nominee-controlled) to co-mingle proceeds of illegal logging, mining or waste trafficking with legitimate business accounts.

citations.quote: criminals used front companies to co-mingle gains from illegal mining, logging and waste trafficking into their legitimate business accounts

indicators.description: Logging-sector companies with frequent transactions to offshore financial centres.

citations.quote: Companies operating in the logging sector with frequent transactions to offshore financial centres.

indicators.description: Large cash withdrawals from financial institutions operating in rural areas near known illegal mining or logging zones.

citations.quote: Large cash withdrawals from financial institutions operating in rural areas that may be in proximity to illegal mining or logging areas.

extraction_notes: This is a broad FATF thematic report covering three distinct predicate crime types (illegal logging/land clearing, illegal mining, waste trafficking); typologies extracted are those the report develops in depth with dedicated sections/case studies rather than every risk indicator in Annex A. The 'Money Laundering from Environmental Crime' label is proposed as emergent because no existing Knowledge Centre typology captures environmental crime as the underlying predicate driver -- reviewers may wish to consider whether this should instead be modelled as a new family. The Gertler/Steinmetz/Kabila corruption cases (Annex C) are illustrative examples cited by the report rather than the report's central case studies; sanctions_desk routing reflects Gertler's Global Magnitsky designation mentioned in the text. Country list under jurisdictions covers only those tied to named cases/examples, not the full list of ~45 countries that responded to FATF's survey.
